title_ru: Гигантская тыква победила на ярмарке в Миллбруке
description_ru: Вымышленная новость: пенсионер вырастил рекордную тыкву весом 412 килограммов, и весь город гордится им.
text:
A small farming town called Millbrook has a new world champion. On Saturday, a retired bus driver named Harold Pennick won the Giant Vegetable Show with a pumpkin that weighed 412 kilograms. It is the heaviest pumpkin that anyone in the country has ever grown, and the people of Millbrook are very proud.

The show takes place every September in the village hall, and this year more than two thousand visitors came. Many of them travelled from other towns to see the huge vegetables. There were long carrots, enormous onions and cabbages as big as car tyres. But when the judges arrived at Harold's table, everybody stopped talking. The pumpkin was orange, round and almost as tall as a small child. It took six strong men and a special truck to bring it into the hall.

"I could not believe my eyes," said Dorothy Wren, the head judge. "I have been doing this job for twenty-two years, and I have never seen anything bigger. When we put it on the scale, the numbers kept going up and up. Then we all started to clap." The old record was 389 kilograms, and Harold broke it by more than twenty kilograms.

Harold is seventy years old, and he began growing vegetables only five years ago, after he stopped driving buses. He says that his secret is patience. "A pumpkin is like a baby," he explained with a smile. "You have to feed it, give it water and talk to it every day." Harold admits that he spoke to his pumpkin for about an hour each morning. He told it stories about his life, and he sometimes played quiet music on a small radio. His neighbours thought he was a little crazy, but now they are asking him for advice.

The preparation was not easy. Last spring, Harold planted the seed in a special mixture of soil and horse manure. He covered the young plant with a plastic tent to protect it from the cold. In June, he found that the pumpkin was growing about fifteen kilograms every week. He built a roof over it, because he was afraid of heavy rain and hungry birds. In August, a storm nearly destroyed his garden, and Harold slept outside in a chair for three nights to guard the plant. "My wife said that I was more worried about the pumpkin than about her," he laughed.

The pumpkin, which Harold named Big Bertha, is now the most popular visitor in town. On Sunday morning, hundreds of people stood in a line outside the hall to take photographs with it. Children climbed on a small ladder to touch it, and the local baker offered to make the biggest pumpkin pie in history. The mayor, Gerald Foxley, said that the town is going to hold a special party next week. "Millbrook has always been a quiet place," he said. "Now we are famous, and it is much better than I expected."

Harold won a golden cup, a certificate and a prize of two thousand pounds. He says that he is not going to spend the money on himself. Instead, he plans to buy new books for the school library and to give some to the village hall, where the roof leaks. "I have everything I need," he said. "I only wanted to prove that an old man can still do something amazing."

Not everybody was happy about the result, however. A farmer from the neighbouring village, Walter Dunn, finished in second place with a pumpkin of 380 kilograms. He said that he was pleased for his rival but also a little jealous. "Next year I am going to grow a bigger one," he promised. "I have already ordered better seeds." Harold only smiled and said that he was ready for the challenge.

Experts say that giant vegetable growing is becoming more popular. Dr Helen Marsh, who teaches plant science at a university, explained that a giant pumpkin can grow more than a kilogram every hour in the best conditions. "It is one of the fastest-growing things on Earth," she said. "Growers need good soil, plenty of water and a lot of luck with the weather."

What will happen to Big Bertha now? Harold has some ideas. The seeds are the most valuable part, and many growers want to buy them. He will keep some for himself, and he will give a few to local schools so that children can try to grow their own giants. The rest of the pumpkin, he says, will become soup for the whole town at the party next Saturday. "That is the best end for a champion," he said. "And it is going to be a very big pot."

questions.question: What was Harold's secret?
questions.answer: Patience: he fed it, gave it water and talked to it every day.

questions.question: What happened in August?
questions.answer: A storm nearly destroyed his garden, so he slept outside for three nights to guard the plant.

questions.question: What will happen to the pumpkin after the show?
questions.answer: Some seeds will go to schools, and the rest will become soup for the whole town.
